ledger.claim: A device's maker can disable features after sale.
ledger.request_basis: when its maker can disable features after sale

sentences.text: The receipt's in your pocket, the box is in your car, and somewhere in a data center you've never visited, there's a switch that determines whether your purchase actually works.
You didn't buy a product.
You bought a seat at a table where the host reserves the right to pull your chair out whenever it suits him.
Take the house you've owned for twenty years.
You paid the price, signed the deed, collected the keys (and probably the low-grade dread that comes with every major appliance failure).
The seller can't come back in year three to remove the plumbing because they've decided to monetize water differently.
That'd be fraud.
The deed is the deed, and ownership means the transfer of control, not just the transfer of a receipt.
Now picture the device you carry.
The company that made it can push a firmware update that disables features you relied on yesterday.
Not because those features failed.
Because the company determined that your continued free use of them conflicted with a new licensing arrangement, a product launch, or a revenue model that didn't exist when you paid.
The physical object is yours – what it does is theirs, on terms they can revise at will.
This is the architecture they've designed for you.
You're buying hardware (which they've agreed to let you keep) and renting capability (which they never disclosed as a rental).
"License," "service," "platform" – these are the words their legal team chose to make tenancy look like ownership.
That confusion isn't accidental.
It's the product.
I've read enough of these update notices to recognize the pattern, and I'd guess you have too.

They've been doing this long enough that it barely registers as news: a feature disappears, the update notes call it a "change to improve your experience," and most of us shrug and move on because the alternative is arguing with a terms-of-service agreement the size of a mortgage document.
What does this cost us?
We lose the secondary market that lets you sell the thing you bought.
We lose the repair shop that can fix it without a manufacturer blessing.
We lose your ability to hand it to someone who can't afford the current model.
And we lose something harder to name: the assurance, which we once took for granted, that the device you bought today will do what it does today.
A device that can be retroactively redefined is a device that never fully disclosed its terms at the point of sale.
That's not a purchase.
That's an ongoing negotiation where only one party gets to make offers.
The companies running this arrangement will tell you it's about security updates and protecting your data.
That's obviously true in the way that a landlord's fire-code compliance is true (required, yes, and also awfully convenient for someone who'd prefer you never leave).
What it's actually about is maintaining a revenue stream past the point of sale.
I mean this precisely.
If they can keep a hand on the device after you've paid, they can keep extracting from you indefinitely, on their schedule, at their discretion.
What's the honest term for that?
Not ownership – an installment plan where the installments never stop and the company decides when you've paid enough.
I think calling it a sale is bullshit.
The receipt in your pocket used to mean something specific.
It meant you'd exchanged money for an object, and the object was now yours to use, modify, sell, or break – without asking permission, without checking in.
What it means now is that you've paid for the right to operate something on terms you didn't negotiate and can't change.
The switch is still there.
I call that a landlord with better PR.
